report.source_text: On day 12 he was referred to liaison psychiatry due to poor engagement in rehabilitation. He was diagnosed with adjustment disorder, started on the antidepressant citalopram and discharged back to the stroke team. He was re-referred to liaison psychiatry 10 days later, when he presented with irritability, aggression and sexual disinhibition. A small dose of olanzapine was started. The contemporary hospital records describe disorientation, distractibility, confabulation, paranoid affect, and verbal and physical aggression. Olanzapine was increased and citalopram was stopped as it was feared that it may have triggered a manic episode.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 39-year-old man presented in March 2020 with malaise, fever, cough, and severe hypoxia due to COVID-19 pneumonia confirmed by positive swab and chest X-ray showing peripheral opacities. By day 8, he developed neurological deterioration including reduced GCS, right-sided weakness, hemisensory loss, and diplopia. Cognitive testing revealed broad impairments on admission to the neurobehavioral unit. Brain MRI with gadolinium demonstrated multiple acute ischaemic infarctions in the posterior circulation. Magnetic resonance angiography revealed multifocal narrowing and occlusions in bilateral posterior cerebral arteries suggestive of CNS vasculitis likely secondary to COVID-19. CSF analysis showed mildly raised protein but was negative for common viral pathogens and lacked SARS-CoV-2 testing. He received a short 3-day course of methylprednisolone for suspected CNS vasculitis. Subsequently, he developed neuropsychiatric symptoms managed with psychotropics. Neurological rehabilitation over two weeks led to rapid cognitive improvements with residual mild-moderate deficits. Despite extensive workup and treatment, final multidisciplinary consensus favored CNS vasculopathy over vasculitis, but no biopsy or formal final report documented.
